pronunciation.approximation: aw-GOON, low tone on the first syllable, high on the last.
pronunciation.note: Ògún carries Yoruba's tonal low-high melody: ò with the grave (low tone), gún with the acute (high) — the tones are phonemic, and the restoration keeps both exactly as the language requires. The name is bound to the word for iron (irin) in his praise-names: "Ogun, master of iron, the one who clears the road."

domains.title: The Road-Opener
domains.subtitle: Iron, War, Labour, and the First Path through the Forest
domains.lead: Ògún is the orisha of iron and of every road iron opens: the hunter who cleared the primordial forest so the gods could descend, the smith who arms the farmer and the warrior alike, and the patron of every worker who makes a living by metal — from the blacksmith to the surgeon to the driver.

cards.name: The Cutlass
cards.desc: His tool and emblem: the blade that clears the forest path — creation by cutting.

cards.name: The Forge
cards.desc: The smith's fire: iron is his body, and every smithy his shrine.

cards.name: The First Road
cards.desc: He hacked the road through the primal forest that let the orisha reach the earth.

cards.name: The Dog
cards.desc: His companion and sacrifice — the hunter's faithful one, honoured at his festivals.

symbols.name: The cutlass
symbols.meaning: The path-making blade — technology as the opener of ways

symbols.name: The anvil
symbols.meaning: The forge's heart, where his power is hammered into tools

symbols.name: The palm wine
symbols.meaning: His drink — offered by hunters and smiths for coolness and courage

symbols.name: The dog
symbols.meaning: The hunter's companion and the sacrifice his festivals accept — loyalty that follows the road even into the earth

symbols.name: The iron itself
symbols.meaning: His praise-names say it plainly: the metal is the god's body and his dwelling among men

mythology.lead: Ògún's myths are the Yoruba meditation on power: the strength that clears the way for everyone, and the rage that, unmastered, turns on its own town.

myths.title: The First Road
myths.text: When the orisha first sought to descend from heaven to the unfinished earth, the primordial forest stood unbroken and no god could pass — not even the greatest among them, for all their wisdom. Ògún took his cutlass and cut the road through, and the gods followed him down (the tradition preserved by E. B. Idowu in Olódùmarè, 1962, and sung in the Ifá odù Ogunda, ‘Ògún creates’). The detail the storytellers never drop is the technology: where other cosmogonies begin with a word or a combat, the Yoruba world begins with a blade — creation as clearance, being as path. Yet ritual order keeps its own counsel: Èṣù-Ẹlẹ́gbá, not Ògún, is propitiated first in every rite, for the road-opener opens ways that others must keep. The myth encodes an entire philosophy of work: civilisation is something hacked out of chaos, by someone, with a tool — and the hacker is owed his portion forever after.

myths.title: The King of Irè
myths.text: Installed as king of Irè, Ògún came one festival day to find his people silent — the honours due him unperformed (the Irè tradition recorded by Idowu, Olódùmarè). In his rage he drew the sword and cut down his own townsfolk, and the slaughter ended only when he saw his own son among the fallen. Coming to himself, he declared that he would walk no more among men, and sank into the earth — remaining, as the praise-songs say, in the iron itself. Every Ògún festival at Irè replays the king’s coming and going: the worshippers greet him with noise and honour precisely where the myth says silence once killed. The myth does not excuse the rage; it institutionalises the apology — a god whose festival is a town’s vow never again to repeat the silence that set him off.

myths.title: Master of the Forest
myths.text: Before he was king or smith, Ògún was the supreme hunter, lord of the deep forest where no farm grows and no town reaches. The hunters’ guilds sing his oríkì at the forest’s edge — ‘Ògún, the one who has water yet bathes in blood,’ ‘the one whose dog never tires’ — and hunters still pour the first palm wine of the season to him before the first hunt (hunters’ lore collected across Yorubaland; see Awolalu, Yoruba Beliefs and Sacrificial Rites, 1979). The forest is his because the road is his: every path into the bush is a cut he owns, every trap a loan from his forge. The tradition makes him the patron not of hunting’s glamour but of its discipline — the oath-bound guild, the shared kill, the rules that keep the forest from becoming mere wilderness. His hunters do not conquer the bush; they negotiate with it, in his name and under his law.

myths.title: The One Who Followed
myths.text: The corpus preserves, in several variants, the story of the dog. When Ògún had done the terrible thing at Irè and withdrew from men, the one creature that followed him into the wilderness was his dog; in some tellings the dog dies for him, in others it leads him back out of the bush when he is lost past return. The ethnography is plain: dogs are still the sacrifice his festivals accept — the one animal whose death honours rather than offends him (festival practice recorded by Pierre Verger, Orixás, 1981, and J. O. Awolalu, 1979; the black dog of the forge is a standing figure in Cuban patakís, Lydia Cabrera, El Monte, 1954). The sources do not fix one canonical version, and the honest reading keeps the variants side by side. The myth’s theology is of a piece with the rest of him: the god of the road keeps, as his emblem among living things, the one companion that will not leave the road’s end — loyalty itself, paid for in kind.

myths.title: The Trap and the Arrow
myths.text: Ògún’s deepest alliance is with his brother-in-law, the archer Òchósi — and the founding story is a quarrel. Both laid claim to the same kill: Ògún had set the trap, but Òchósi’s arrow had struck the beast, and each argued the kill was his by craft. They took the dispute before the council of orisha, which ruled that the meat belonged to both — and bound them thereafter as partners in every hunt, the smith whose iron holds and the hunter whose aim decides (the tale survives in Yoruba hunters’ lore and in the Cuban patakís collected by Cabrera, El Monte). The myth is a treatise on technology: the trap without the arrow is a cage, the arrow without the trap is a shot in the dark. Yoruba religion enshrines the lesson in devotion itself — the two orisha are worshipped together to this day, and no serious hunter’s shrine to one lacks the other.

lore.syncretism: The Middle Passage carried him across the Atlantic, where the iron god found new irons: in Cuban Santería he is Oggún, syncretized with Saint Peter (keeper of the keys — the metal of heaven's gate) or Saint George; in Brazilian Candomblé, Ògún is Saint George of the dragon-slaying spear; in Haitian Vodou he is Ogou Feray, the warrior-loa of the forge and the soldier's flag. The saints changed the face; the iron, the road, and the dog kept the god.
lore.culturalLegacy: Nigeria's Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka is his most famous devotee: Ògún is the patron of Soyinka's art — the road-maker who is also the destroyer — and the essay "The Fourth Stage" and the novel The Road are his modern liturgy. Ògún state in Nigeria bears his name; his praise-names echo in the foundries and mechanics' yards of every Yoruba city, where a splash of palm wine on the anvil still opens the working day.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ògún is the god of the tool in the hand. Every technology is his: the blade that clears the road and the blade that clears the town are the same iron, and only the wielder's self-command decides which road it opens. He asks the maker's question, which is also the warrior's and the surgeon's: what does your strength serve — and who stands in the way when it slips?

Every driver who splashes gin on a bumper in Lagos, every mechanic who taps the anvil before the first weld, is keeping his liturgy without needing its name: tools are moral — they open roads or open wounds — and the hand must be steadier than the blade. Ògún's myth admits what no other war-god's does: that the rage is his own. The road-opener who cut down his own town is the honest patron of a technological age: the strength is real, the forest is real, and so is the apology owed when the blade turns.

Soyinka, his greatest modern devotee, calls him the god of the road and of transition — the patron of everyone who makes a path where none existed, and the warning that every path is cut through something. In the diaspora's forge-altars the lesson survives translation: iron does not apologize, but it must be answered for. The road-opener asks of every builder, coder, and driver the same question his own myth could not escape: when the forest is cleared, what will you plant — and whom did the clearing cost?

The anvil rings, the day's first iron is cut, and the road — his road — opens another meter. The forest always grows back; that is why the clearing is a daily act, and why the god of the cutlass is worshipped not once but every working morning.

lore.archaeology: Yorubaland is one of Africa's oldest iron-working regions: the smelting furnaces of the Nsukka plateau (Lejja) date the craft back over two thousand years, and the guild-smithies of the forest belt kept the ritual side — the first iron of a furnace smelted with prayers to Ògún. His shrines are often the anvil itself; the great festivals of Ire and of Ọndó preserve the masquerades and the dog-sacrifice described in the earliest ethnographies, and the odù Ogunda verses are still divined daily by babaláwo across the Yoruba world.
lore.originalScriptNote: Yoruba is written in Latin letters with tone marks — the orthography the restoration preserves: Ò (low tone) and ú (high tone) are the name as spoken. In the Ifá divination corpus his signs live in the odù Ogunda, "Ogun creates," one of the sixteen principal odù: the god written into the divination system itself.
